# Known divergences from the reference deobfuscator: Unpack

Untwist's unpack stage is verified against the reference deobfuscator by `cargo xtask diff-unpack`; the items below are deliberate, not bugs.

- Module paths are stored in one normalised POSIX form with **no `./` prefix** (`3.js`, `index.js`, `node_modules/lib/index.js`), so `bundle.json` reads `"path": "3.js"` where the reference deobfuscator writes `"path": "./3.js"`. The file names on disk are identical, and `ModulePaths::specifier` re-adds the `./` when a specifier is emitted, so a generated `require("…")` or `import … from "…"` is byte-identical to the reference deobfuscator's except where the next item says otherwise. The reference deobfuscator is itself inconsistent here: browserify entries are already stored as `index.js` with no prefix while unreachable browserify modules keep `./<id>.js`.
- A specifier for a file under the root `node_modules/` is the bare form (`require("lib/index.js")`) only when node would resolve it to that file. The reference deobfuscator always writes the bare form. Untwist writes the relative path instead (`require("../node_modules/lib/index.js")`) when a file or directory at `<ancestor of the requester>/node_modules/<the same tail>` is also written, a module or an input file copied into the tree beside a partial bundle (node searches those first, and tries `.js`, `.json` and `.node` after the name), when the tail has the shape of a node core module name (`events`, `fs/promises`, anything starting with `node:`; node loads core modules before it looks at `node_modules`), when it starts with `#`, and when the target is not a path the bundle assigned. A sibling path that starts with a dot (`.config/a.js`) gets its `./` too, where the reference deobfuscator leaves a specifier node reads as a package name. All linkers go through `ModulePaths::specifier` in `specifier.rs`; the webpack reference-parity lane keeps the reference deobfuscator's form.
- An AMD or UMD factory that declares a function with the name of one of its parameters (`define(["dep"], function (a) { function a() {} … })`, also inside a block) is refused and the input is left as it is. The lowering turns each parameter into `var a = require(…)` at the top of the module, where the hoisted function would be overwritten by the dependency; in the factory the function wins. The reference deobfuscator does not unpack AMD or UMD.
- `bundle.json` writes `"entryId": null` when no entry module was found; the reference deobfuscator writes the empty string. `entry_id` is an `Option<String>` internally rather than a `''` sentinel.
- `bundle.json` carries two fields the reference deobfuscator does not: `isEntry` per module, and a `chunkIds` array. The reference deobfuscator captures chunk ids in its JSONP matcher and then discards them.
- Cross-chunk requires that cannot be resolved are reported as diagnostic notes (`module <id>: require("<id>") has no module in this bundle`) instead of being injected into the output as a `/*the reference deobfuscator:missing*/` leading comment. `xtask::diff::normalize` prints with comments disabled, so this is a non-difference in the differential test.
- A module id that would escape the output directory (`../tmp.js`, `./\..\node_modules\debug\src\index`) is replaced at path-assignment time with `_unsafe_<sanitised id>.js` plus a note. The reference deobfuscator keeps the traversing path and throws inside `save()`, losing the whole bundle. Two modules that resolve to the same output path are uniquified with `-2`, `-3` stem suffixes and a note; the reference deobfuscator does not detect path collisions at all and silently overwrites.
- Extracted module programs start with a **script** source type, so a module is ESM only after its own `require.r(exports)` call. Untwist's parser tries `SourceType::mjs()` first and keeps it whenever a file has no errors, so inheriting the bundle's source type would mark every module ESM.
- Browserify's `./utils` versus `utils/index.js` ambiguity is resolved by constraint: a module whose path came from an extensionless relative request is moved to `<stem>/index.js` when its own relative requests escape the tree from `<stem>.js` but not from `<stem>/`. The reference deobfuscator marks this case `test.skip` and always produces `utils.js`. The inference is conservative and leaves all three passing `path.test.ts` cases and all four browserify fixtures unchanged.
- Browserify modules are linked through their dependency maps. Each free `require("<request>")` whose request is a key of the module's map is rewritten to the path of the file of the mapped id, so two versions of one package, a bundled shim named like a node core module (`events`, `buffer`) and a module reached by two requests from different directories each load the file the bundle loads. The reference deobfuscator keeps the request as written and relies on the inferred file paths, and so does the reference-parity lane. A local function named `require` is left as written. In the reference-parity lane a computed request and a request outside the map are left as written too; by default the only requests left as written are a node built-in (`fs`, `node:path`), which node resolves the same from any file, and a package request (`vscode`, `@scope/pkg/x`) that node, starting from the written file and walking every `node_modules` folder up to the root of the tree (with node's extensions, index files and `package.json`), would resolve to no file the tree writes. That is decided after every path is final, so a dependency map entry such as `'./node_modules/foo/index.js'`, a `..` request out of a package, an unreached module named after its id and a library label all count; module naming does not move a library module into the folder of a package that a request left as written names, and when a written file still answers such a request the bundle is refused (`module <id>: require("foo") is left as written, which node would resolve to a file of the written tree; no bundle is written (node_modules/foo/index.js)`). Any other request the map does not send to a module of the bundle refuses the bundle (`module <id>: it requires "./a", which neither its dependency map nor the bundle holds, so the written files would not load what the bundle loads; no bundle is written`): browser-pack hands such a request to the require function around the bundle, while in the tree node would resolve it next to the written file, often to a file written from another module. The same note covers a computed request, a request named like an `Object.prototype` property that the map only inherits (`constructor`), a map entry that sends a request to an id the bundle lacks or to a falsy id (`0`, `""`, which browser-pack reads as the request itself), a module id named like an `Object.prototype` property (browser-pack's `{}` cache already holds it, so the module never runs), an entry id that is not a module, a factory that is async, a generator or takes a pattern or default parameter (browser-pack's `.call` does not run those like a file), a module map or dependency map that names one key twice (the object keeps the last value, `undefined` included), and a factory that reads a `require` it does not bind itself, in its code or through a constant `eval` whose payload names `require` (`function (r, m, e) { require("./b") }` or `eval("require('./b')")`: in the bundle that is the require around the bundle, in the written file node's own). A request outside the map that names a module id, and a renamed `require` that is still called after linking, are reported as notes. When the bundle lists several entries (`[1,7]`), `index.js` ends with a `require` of each later entry in order; when the entry module may return early or binds `require` itself, the later entries are not run and a note says so. The reference deobfuscator runs only the first entry.
- Several input files are detected separately and their module maps merged into one bundle before paths are assigned, so a require that crosses a chunk boundary resolves. The reference deobfuscator has no multi-file API; every cross-chunk require becomes a missing marker.
- User path mappings are a closed enum of four shapes (string literal, numeric literal, identifier, `object.property` member) rather than arbitrary `@codemod/matchers` matchers; a regexp-literal matcher is not implemented in v1. A mapping key that matches a second module is skipped and the first module keeps it, where the reference deobfuscator throws `Mapping X is already used.` Mappings that matched nothing become notes; the reference deobfuscator tracks them in a variable it never reads.
- Webpack helpers nobody undoes (`require.t`, `require.e`, `require.S`) and forms this crate did not match (a surviving `require.d`, `require.r` or `require.n`) are reported as notes. The reference deobfuscator leaves them in the output silently.
- In the conservative comparison mode, `convert_default_require` resolves the `require.n` argument and the getter variable by **name** over the whole module program (first `require(<number>)` declarator wins) rather than through scope bindings. A module that shadows one of those names in an inner scope would diverge; webpack's generated names make that unreachable in practice.
- **`require.n` becomes `x.default` only where the target is proven harmony.** The reference deobfuscator turns `var g = require.n(x)` into `var g = x.default` when the required module calls `require.r` anywhere and into `var g = x` otherwise, for numeric ids only. That reads the export once, at the declaration (a circular import or a late `require.d` getter then gives `undefined` where `g()` gave the value), trusts a `.r` on another object or one followed by `module.exports = ...`, and leaves `g()` and `g.a` calls on a string-id bundle with nothing to serve them. By default Untwist rewrites only when the required module is already ESM or starts with `require.r(exports)` and never names `module` or rebinds `exports`/`require`, the getter is declared directly after its `require(id)` (string or numeric id), neither binding is reassigned or redeclared, and every use is `g()` or `g.a`; each use then becomes `x.default` (`(0, x.default)(...)` where it was called) and the getter declaration is dropped, so the export is read when the bundle read it. A module that hands the runtime away (`require` passed on, `require.c`, `require.m`, `eval`, `with`, the factory's `arguments`) stops the rewrite for the whole bundle. Everything else keeps `require.n`, served by the bundle's own helper in `_runtime/webpack.js`. The conservative comparison mode keeps the reference deobfuscator's conversion; the default snapshot of `fixtures/reference/unpack/webpack-esm.js` and `default_require_sees_the_esm_flag_convert_esm_set` were re-pinned.
- **A local or parameter named `require` is not the runtime.** A by-name rewrite of `require(<id>)`, `require.n(...)` and `require.t(...)` also rewrites `function load(require) { return require("./utils") + require(7); }` inside a module, whose arguments then become module paths the function was never given. Untwist asks one question, `scan::is_free`, in the require-path rewriter, the `.n` conversion, the `.t` conversion and the host-`require` shield: a reference that scoping resolves to a binding of the module is left alone, and a node without a reference (one Untwist built itself) counts as the runtime. This holds in both modes, so the conservative comparison mode differs from a by-name rewrite only inside a module that declares its own `require`.
- **A webpack var injection is spliced only where it is proven.** The reference deobfuscator turns every module statement of the form `(function (a, b) { ... }).call(this, x, y)` (or `.call(exports, ...)`) into `var a = x; var b = y;` followed by the body. That changes the program when the call is not the whole module (its declarations join the module's, a `return` now ends the module), when the counts differ, when the body has a directive, a `return` at its own level, `arguments`, `new.target` or `eval`, when a name the body declares at its own level collides with a parameter or with `module`/`exports`/`require`/`__filename`/`__dirname` (a function declaration is hoisted above the new `var` and loses to it), when an argument reads a parameter name or a name the body declares, or when the receiver is `exports` and the body reads `this`. By default Untwist splices only webpack's own wrapper: an anonymous plain function called as the last statement of a module whose other statements are `require.r(exports)`, with as many arguments as plain, distinct parameters and none of the cases above. Any other call stays as written. The conservative comparison mode keeps the reference deobfuscator's splice.
- **A webpack or browserify bundle is taken only when every factory is closed.** The reference deobfuscator finds these bundle shapes anywhere in the program and lifts each factory body into its own file. A factory that reads a binding of the scope around the bundle (a variable beside a nested bundle call, a parameter of the function around it, the `__WEBPACK_EXTERNAL_MODULE_x__` parameters of a `libraryTarget: "umd"` wrapper with externals, a name of the bundle's own prelude), its own `arguments`, a parameter the runtime never passes, or that calls `eval` directly (any call spelled `eval(...)`, also through a local binding named `eval`) or holds a `with` statement (the module rewrites cannot be proven inside one; a direct `eval` of a constant string that declares nothing and reads only names no binding holds at the call, such as `eval("Math;")`, is allowed, and those names are then kept free in the written file: a factory parameter is renamed around them, and a bundle whose rewrites would bind one is not written; such an eval whose names include `require`, `module`, `exports`, `__filename` or `__dirname` is refused, since it reads the name the bundle file has and the written file would answer for itself: `eval("require('./b')")` counts as a free-require read, `it reads require, which every module has for itself`, except that in a webpack factory an eval whose whole payload is `require` (`eval("require;")("worker_threads")`, which real bundles use to hide node's require from the bundler) is the host's `require` and is judged by the webpack rule below; a factory that reads a free `module` or `exports` in its code while its own parameter in that place has another name is refused too, since the written file would bind that name: `it reads exports, which every module has for itself`; so is a factory that reads a free `__filename` or `__dirname`, in both lanes: in the bundle every module sees the bundle file and its directory, in the tree each written file sees itself, so two modules that shared one directory would disagree (`it reads __dirname, which every module has for itself`); a webpack factory may use the host's free `require` only as `typeof require` or as the callee of a call with one literal request naming a node built-in other than `module` and `process`, or a package (webpack's externals, also through a choice such as `(typeof require == "undefined" ? __webpack_require__(125) : require)("worker_threads")`); every other appearance, in the body or a parameter, is refused: a relative request, any member of `require` (`require.main`, `require.resolve`, `require.cache`, `require.valueOf()`, which hands the function back, `require.__defineGetter__` and `require.prototype`, which write to it, a computed member), a write, `require` as a value or an alias, since node answers them from the written file's path or gives each written file its own function: `it uses the host's require (require.valueOf), which a written file answers for its own path`; a package request kept this way is resolved from the written file like browserify's left requests, and a request node would answer with a file of the written tree refuses the bundle), then runs in a file where none of that exists. By default Untwist checks every factory with the rule the other bundlers already follow (`closed.rs`: only globals, the mapped parameters and the factory's own declarations) and, when one fails, takes no bundle from that shape: the program is output whole, with the note `module <id> is not closed over its own scope; no bundle is written: it reads <name>, a binding of the bundle's scope`. A later shape in the same file whose factories are closed is still found, and is written only under the rule for code beside the bundle below. A UMD wrapper with externals is refused this way for now rather than having its externals turned into requires. The conservative comparison mode keeps the reference deobfuscator's behaviour.
- **A request a module leaves to node must resolve alike from the bundle and from the written tree.** node resolves `require(...)` and `import(...)` from the file that holds the call, so a relative request, or any route whose answer depends on the module's own file or the main module's, gives the bundle's answer in the bundle and the written file's in the tree; a route relative to the working directory is the same on both sides. In every bundle kind, a host `require("x")` a module keeps (webpack externals, esbuild's and Bun's `require` and `__require`, rolldown, UMD factories, Rollup, Parcel's hoisted output, AMD, Closure, Metro, Turbopack, SystemJS) and every `import("x")`, static `import … from "x"` and `export … from "x"` in a module or in the code kept beside the bundle, also an `import()` in the text of a constant `eval`, must name a node built-in other than `module` and `process` (which hand out `createRequire`, `_load`, `_resolveFilename` and `mainModule`), or a package; the one exception is the recorded runtime line `import { createRequire } from "node:module"` whose binding only feeds `createRequire(import.meta.url)` (rolldown's and esbuild's `require` shim). An `import()` of a non-literal specifier refuses the bundle, and in the default lane so does every relative request in an `import()`, a static `import` or an `export … from` (`module 0 uses import("./1.js"), which node answers from the file that holds it, so the written file would not load what the bundle loads; no bundle is written`), also when it names an input of the run: a mirrored input is a second copy, so a chunk that imports the bundle's input back by name evaluates the whole bundle again, node reads the specifier as a URL (`%6C`, `?x`, `#x`) and through symbolic links, and the target's own imports are not followed. The vite 8, rolldown, esbuild and Bun ESM splits given with their chunks are therefore kept whole in the default lane. Under `--unsafe` such a relative request is kept when the bundle is one input of a run whose other inputs are mirrored, the module that holds it is written in the directory of that input, the specifier holds no `%`, `?`, `#` or `\`, and it names a mirrored input other than the bundle's own; and the bundle is refused when any other input of the run names the bundle's input in a relative request. The lane's premise is that the inputs given beside a bundle are the files its relative imports load, and that the bundle's input is not imported back by name through a route that check does not see. In the default lane a module or the code beside the bundle that holds a code runner (`Function`, `new Function`, `.constructor(…)` on a function value, indirect `eval`, a timer given a string) refuses the bundle unless the runner's text is constant and parses free of `import()`, `import.meta`, `require`, `module`, `exports`, `process`, `__filename`, `__dirname`, `globalThis`, `global`, a computed member and other runners (`Function("return this")` is kept); a runner taken as a value refuses, and so does a request for the `vm` built-in. A direct `eval` keeps the scan of its constant text. Under `--unsafe` the premise is that no code text reaches `import()`, node's module objects or loader. In the default lane the own file's and the main file's names are closed off by an allow-list: `import.meta` may appear only as `typeof import.meta` or inside the recorded runtime line's `createRequire(import.meta.url)`; a member of a free `process` only from a fixed list of members that name no file (`env`, `nextTick`, `platform`, `version`, `versions`, `cwd`, `exit`, the event methods, the standard streams, …; not `argv`, `mainModule` or `getBuiltinModule`); a member of a free `module` only as `exports`, `hot` or `loaded`; a member of the host's free `require` only as `apply`; `__filename` and `__dirname` not at all. Anything else (`import.meta.url`, `import.meta.filename`, `require.main`, `module.filename`, `module.id`, `module.parent`, `process.argv`) refuses the bundle. Under `--unsafe` the premise is that the program does not read its own file name or the main module's path. `require("module")` refuses the bundle too. Each kept package request is resolved like browserify's left requests (`crates/untwist-unpack/src/browserify/resolve.rs`): it refuses the bundle when a file of the written tree or any input of the run lies on node's lookup path for it, looked up from the written file and also from the bundle's own input as named under the directory the inputs share, which is where a partial run mirrors the other inputs (`app/bundle.js` beside `app/node_modules/foo/index.js` refuses: `module 1: require("foo") is left as written, which node would resolve to a file of the written tree`). A module that names `process.mainModule`, `process.getBuiltinModule` or a computed member of `process` is refused in both lanes. Turbopack's server runtime is not checked: it is an input written whole at its own path (a fixed path, which refuses the bundle if anything would move it), so its chunk loads run from the same place on both sides. `process` taken as a value is not followed, nor is it reached through the global object (`var p = process; p.mainModule.require("./1.js")` is the premise row `r4n10`; `globalThis.process.mainModule` and `global.process.mainModule` are the same premise): bundles pass `process` to their polyfills and destructure it (`const { env } = process`), so the README states the premise that no code reaches node's module objects or loader that way. A factory or module wrapper that is async, a generator, or takes a pattern, rest or default parameter is refused in every kind (`its factory is async, a generator or takes a pattern, rest or default parameter, so it does not run like a file`), since the default runs when the bundle calls the factory and the async body would become a file with a top-level `await`. Rows: `crates/untwist-cli/tests/host_routes_review`, `host_routes_mirrored` and `host_routes_split` (`host_route_splits.rs`), both lanes, node parity.
- **A bundle is split in the safe lane only when no module can see its caller.** In the bundle a function called by a module's top-level code has that module's factory as its caller, with the bundle's `module`, `exports` and `require` as the caller's arguments; in a written file the caller is node's module wrapper, with five other arguments. The same holds for every bundle kind: a factory or module wrapper (esbuild's `__commonJS`, Parcel, Metro, Turbopack, AMD, UMD, SystemJS, Closure) or the outer function of a split Rollup bundle is the caller in the bundle and not in the written files. No scan of property names can prove that nothing reads that frame (a computed key, a reader passed around as a value, text built at run time, `Error.prepareStackTrace` with `getFunction()`, `with (f) caller` in another input), so by default Untwist relies on how V8 treats strict code instead: the `caller` of a function whose caller is strict code is `null`, reading `caller` or `arguments` of a strict function throws, and `getFunction()` and `getThis()` are `undefined` for strict frames (and for every frame once a strict one is on the stack). This was checked in node 22 for `f.caller`, `arguments.callee.caller`, `with (f) caller`, `({ __proto__: f }).caller`, `getFunction()` from `Error.prepareStackTrace` and from `Error.captureStackTrace`. A bundle is therefore split only when every function in the input that holds it is strict code (the input is an ES module or starts with `"use strict"`, or each function sits in a function or class that is strict) and every written module file is strict code (it has `import` or `export`, is `.mjs`, or starts with `"use strict"`). Untwist adds `"use strict"` to a written file only when the module's code was already strict in the bundle (see below), never to code that was sloppy there. Otherwise no bundle is written, with the note `the bundle is not strict code, <the function F on line N> is sloppy: a function the modules call could read its caller (...), which is the bundle's own function in the bundle and node's module wrapper in the written files; no bundle is written (--unsafe assumes no such read reaches a module)`, or `module <id> would be written as a sloppy file (...)` with the same reason. Most webpack 4 bundles, and every bundle with a CommonJS module that is not strict, are kept whole in the safe lane this way. Under `--unsafe`, no read of a function's caller or arguments, in any input of the run, is assumed to reach a bundled module's function, and such bundles are unpacked anyway (Krunker's `kpdData.caller` is game data, but that cannot be proven). In every lane, a module whose code is strict in the bundle (all of it: through its own directive, a `"use strict"` of the file or of a function around it, or an ES module input; a class or a `"use strict"` function among a module's top-level statements makes only its own body strict, never the module) and that would otherwise be written as a sloppy CommonJS file is written with a `"use strict"` directive, as esbuild, AMD and Turbopack modules already were; webpack's and browserify's module files used to lose a strictness they had only from the code around them (webpack 5 node chunks and `output.module` chunks start with `"use strict"` and their factories have none), and a factory's own directives now stay in its written file (browserify's were dropped). The input counts as an ES module when it is named `.mjs` or its original text, before any pass runs, does not parse as a script but parses as a module (`import`/`export`, `import.meta` or a top-level `await x`: node 22's syntax detection; `await (x)`, a call of a global named `await`, keeps a script), even when a later pass removes that code (`if (0) { import.meta; }`); every bundle kind in such an input then writes strict module files (browserify's proof refuses it instead). A bundle whose written CommonJS module file (one without `import`/`export`, or the written runtime) would hold `import.meta` or a top-level `await` is not written, in every lane, with the note `module <id> would be written with import.meta, which node runs only in an ES module and the written file cannot keep as the input had it`: node runs a `.js` file with that syntax as an ES module, where `module`, `exports` and `require` do not exist. esbuild's `__commonJS` factory check refuses `import.meta` too. A file written as an ES module keeps its `import.meta` (the `createRequire(import.meta.url)` banner of esbuild and Rolldown ESM output, the one Untwist writes for an ES module entry); its `url` then names the written file, as `__filename` does in a CommonJS file. With several inputs this is decided for each input by its own text and name. A runtime helper that calls `eval` directly, holds a `with` statement, or names the written runtime's own `__webpack_module_paths__` is not moved to `_runtime/webpack.js`, and a module that reads `__dirname` or `__filename` stays CommonJS.
- **A member of `module` used as a call or tag target keeps the bundle whole in every wrapper format.** `module.exports()`, `module["exports"]()`, `(module.exports)()`, `module?.exports()` and `` module.exports`x` `` hand the module object over as `this`: the bundler's record (`{ exports }`) in the bundle, node's `Module` in a written file. Besides webpack and browserify (below), esbuild's and rolldown's `__commonJS` factories, Parcel, Metro and Turbopack modules that do this are not split. `module.exports.f()`, `(0, module.exports)()` and `new module.exports()` hand over no module and are not affected. An AMD factory never gets a module record (a `"module"` dependency is refused), a UMD wrapper and Bun hand over node's own module, Rollup's CommonJS wrappers keep their `{ exports }` holder in the same written file, and SystemJS and Closure modules have no module object.
- **Code beside a webpack or browserify bundle goes into the written entry, or no bundle is written.** When the bundle is one top-level statement of a file that has others, the reference deobfuscator writes the modules and loses the rest, so `node index.js` does not run it. Untwist puts the statements before the bundle at the top of the entry module's file and those after it at its end, which runs them in the same order. That needs the statements not to declare anything at the top level (a `var`, `let`, `const`, function or class, also a `var` or function in a block), not to read `this`, `arguments`, `module`, `exports`, `require`, `__filename`, `__dirname` or a binding of the bundle's own statement, not to call `eval` directly or hold a `with` statement, the bundle to come from one input with one entry, and the entry module to be CommonJS (an ES module's imports would run first), written exactly as strict as that code (the entry file's strictness is decided first, from the bundle, and code from a sloppy top level never goes into a `"use strict"` entry file, nor strict code into a sloppy one), without a `return` at its top level and without a top-level binding of a name that code reads as a global. Otherwise no bundle is written (`the program runs code beside the bundle (line N) that the written files cannot hold: it <why>`, or `... that the written entry cannot hold: <why>`). A file with a second, refused bundle beside a closed one is therefore kept whole too. The bundle must also be the whole of its top-level statement: the statement may wrap it only in `!` or `void` (which run none of the bundle value's code, unlike `+`, `-` or `~`), parentheses, or a function called on the spot whose body holds nothing but the bundle (and directives): a plain function or arrow (not `async`, not a generator) without parameters, called with no arguments or only `this` and literals, directly or with `.call`, or with `.apply` and at most one argument. The exceptions are a webpack 5 library build whose wrapper equals a recorded library wrapper (above), browserify's standalone frame, and a UMD wrapper (webpack 4 `umd`) whose parameters are plain names without defaults and whose CommonJS branch, `module.exports = factory()` with a factory without parameters, is taken before any `typeof define` test, since code before the bundle can define `define`, and only when nothing before the wrapper can run (directives, function declarations and `var` declarations whose initialisers neither call nor write), since such code could change what the wrapper's tests and arguments read (`Object.prototype.nodeName`, a getter on `self`). A bundle inside an `if`, a block, a function that is only declared, any other UMD or library wrapper (an AMD test first), an assignment or a declaration, or a wrapper with other statements beside the bundle (`(function () { f(); <bundle> })()`), means no bundle (`the bundle sits inside a top-level statement (line N) that runs other code too, which the written files cannot hold`), in every lane. A sequence `f(), <bundle>` is split into statements before the unpack stage and follows the rule for code beside the bundle. Not covered: a webpack 5 runtime written at the top level of the file.
- **A webpack runtime is rewritten only when it is proven to be webpack's.** The reference deobfuscator finds the require function by its `modules[id].call(...)` dispatch and keeps the prelude's `require.x = ...` statements, dropping every other prelude statement. By default Untwist first checks the prelude: the require function must be webpack's caching form (the cache lookup, `cache[id] = { exports: {} }` with optional `i`/`l`/`id`/`loaded`, the dispatch, the loaded flag, `return module.exports`); every other statement must be a declaration with a value that runs nothing, a `require.x = <value that runs nothing>` definition (at the top level or in a plain zero-argument wrapper, at most once per name), one of webpack's `__dirname` guards, one entry call (`require(require.s = id)`, a single top-level `require(id)` or the webpack 5 inline entry), or `module.exports = <the entry's exports>`. The require function is used only as a callee, a member object, `typeof` or the receiver of `.bind`, and a helper is never written anywhere but its definition. A helper that reads a binding from around the bundle, the prelude's `this` or `arguments`, `new.target` or `import.meta`, or the host `require`, is not moved. A module that reads or writes a member of its require function that is not a moved helper, passes the require function on, or reaches it through a computed key, means no bundle (`module <id> uses its require function in a way the unpacked files cannot share`). `require.d`/`.r`/`.n`/`.o`/`.t` get webpack's meaning (exports, interop) only when the bundle's own definitions are webpack's recorded texts (`webpack/forms.rs`); otherwise the modules keep the calls, served by the bundle's own helpers. Any other prelude gives the note `the prelude is not proven to be webpack's runtime; no bundle is written: <why>`. Two inputs whose runtimes define a helper differently are not merged (`two webpack runtimes differ`); a module id two chunks define with different text is not merged (webpack keeps the last one loaded); a JSONP chunk whose third element is not webpack 4's deferred-entry list is refused, and a chunk with deferred entries is not merged with a runtime. A module that reads a member of its `module` parameter other than `exports` and `loaded`, reaches it through a computed key, or uses `module` as a value (`module = require.nmd(module)`, `var m = module`) means no bundle (`uses its module object`): in the bundle `module` is webpack's `{ exports }` record, in a written file it is node's `Module` with `parent`, `id`, `filename`, `children`, `paths` and `require`. webpack 4's own `buildin/module.js` and `buildin/harmony-module.js` polyfills are the exception: when a module hands `require(<polyfill>)(module)` straight to a function it calls on the spot (webpack's var injection, a UMD wrapper, also as `false || module`), and every use of that value, through such calls, is `typeof`, a read of `.loaded`, or (for `buildin/module.js` only) a read or write of `.exports`, the written file passes node's `module` itself instead of the polyfilled record: those uses see the same thing in both, and nothing else can reach the record. The polyfill module must equal a form recorded from webpack 4.47.0 (`webpack/buildin.rs`, from `fixtures/webpack-buildin`, raw and as the unpack stage sees it in each lane). Under `--unsafe` (built-ins are not patched), a module may also read other members of the polyfilled value (`.require`, `.paths`, `.children`, `.nodeType`, `.webpackPolyfill`, ...): then the written file does not pass node's `module` but calls the polyfill on webpack's record, written out as `{ get l() { return module.loaded; }, get exports() { return module.exports; }, set exports(value) { module.exports = value; } }`, so `.require` is `undefined` as in the bundle. This needs the one polyfill call of the module to run at most once (in the module's own code, not inside a function, class or loop), since the bundle polyfills its one record while the written file would build a new one each time (`a webpack module polyfill call that can run more than once`). Calling a member read through the record (`m.require(x)`) is allowed, since `this` is then the polyfilled record in both. This needs the proven require function to give the record the `l` flag and exactly one polyfill call in the module; `.i`, `.id` and the names of `Object.prototype` (`hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`, `__lookupGetter__`, ...) still refuse, since those would show the record's own keys or its accessors. In the default lane any such read keeps the refusal (a patched `Object.prototype` getter could tell the objects apart). Besides member reads, the value may be used where only its truthiness counts (an `if`, loop or `?:` test, `!`, the left of `&&`), where it is thrown away (an expression statement, a variable that is never read, in a program with no direct eval or `with`), or handed to a function called on the spot that takes no parameters and does not read `arguments` (webpack's AMD `define` lowering, `function () { ... }.call(exports, require, exports, module)`). Reading `.id` or `.i`, writing anything but `.exports`, using the value any other way, or applying `harmony-module.js` together with another polyfill call keeps the refusal. Uses are checked against an allow-list: `delete`, a member in a destructuring or `for`-`in`/`of` target, a compound or update write, a computed member, or a member used as a call or tag target (which hands the object over as `this`) refuses. A binding that holds the value is skipped as unread only when it is the binding's own declaration (not a redeclared parameter, which `arguments` would alias). A `.loaded` read counts only when the proven require function gives the record the same flag node has: `l: false` set to `true` after the module runs (read through the polyfill's getter), or `loaded: false` set to `true` (read on `module` directly); any other record refuses it. The function the value is handed to must take only plain parameters and not read its own `arguments`. The conservative comparison mode keeps the reference deobfuscator's behaviour, except for the chunk merges.
- **A browserify bundle is taken only when its prelude and its place in the file are browser-pack's.** The reference deobfuscator takes any function with three parameters as the prelude and finds the call anywhere in the program, so a prelude that never runs the modules, runs them in another order or with another `this`, or code before, after or around the call (a condition, an assignment) is lost from the tree. By default Untwist compares the prelude, after renaming every local by its symbol, with the forms recorded from browser-pack 0.9, 2, 3, 5, 6.0 and 6.1 (browserify 2 to 17), raw and minified by terser, uglify-js, esbuild and swc, as the unpack stage sees them in each lane (SHA-256 digests in `browserify/forms.rs`, the texts in `crates/untwist-unpack/tests/data/browserify_forms.txt`; the inputs are `fixtures/browserify-preludes`, generated by `tools/browserify-preludes/gen.mjs` with the pinned tools). The call must be the program's only statement (`!` or `void` in front is allowed) and get browser-pack's arguments: the module map, an empty cache `{}` and a list of literal entry ids. The one other frame is `--standalone`: browserify's UMD head, recorded the same way with its global name left open (one identifier; a dotted name is refused for now), called with an unnamed function that only declares names other than the two the prelude reads (`require`, `Error`) and returns `bundle(<the only entry>)`; the prelude must be one of the forms that returns its require function (eight recorded minified forms of non-standalone bundles return nothing, and the wrapper's call of their result throws). An input whose file runs as an ES module (`.mjs`, or one with module syntax) is strict, while the written files are CommonJS, so it is refused too. Anything else gives `the bundle is not proven to be browserify's output; no bundle is written: <why>`, among them Cocos Creator's `__require` loader, a bundle built with `-r`/`hasExports` (`require=` gives the page a require function other scripts read) and a non-empty cache. The conservative comparison mode keeps the reference deobfuscator's behaviour.
- **No code gives `Object.prototype` a property named like a module id, a chunk id or a request.** webpack 4 (`installedModules[id]`, `installedChunks[chunkId] !== 0` when it loads a chunk or starts deferred modules) and webpack 5 (`__webpack_module_cache__[id] !== undefined`, `installedChunks[chunkId]` in its chunk loaders and `__webpack_require__.O`, and the `{...}[chunkId]` file-name maps of `__webpack_require__.u`) and their chunks, browserify (the prelude's `{}` cache, module map and dependency maps), Parcel (its `cache` and `$parcel$modules` objects and dependency maps) and Turbopack (its `{}` module cache) look modules up in plain objects, so a property, data or accessor, that `Object.prototype` holds under a module id, a chunk id or a request a module passes to its require is found there: the bundle then returns that value, skips the module or takes a chunk as loaded, while node loads the written files through its own cache. Unpacking assumes, in both lanes, that no code makes such a write and does not look for one; `Object.prototype[2] = { exports: "x" }` before `require("./a")` gives `x` in the bundle and module 2's exports in the tree (rows a27, b1-b8 in `crates/untwist-cli/tests/browserify_review`). Checking it would cost nearly every real bundle: the built-ins scan counts every computed read with an unknown key and every alias of `Object.defineProperty` as a possible reach of `Object.prototype`, which browser-pack's own prelude, Babel's interop helpers, lodash and core-js all have. Metro keeps its modules in a `Map`; esbuild, Rollup, rolldown, Bun and Closure output hold each module in a closure, and AMD and SystemJS use the host's loader, so they are not affected. The README lists this premise.
- **No code replaces `Function.prototype.call`, `apply` or `bind`.** browserify's prelude starts each module with `e[i][0].call(...)`, webpack 4 with `modules[moduleId].call(module.exports, ...)`, webpack 5 with `__webpack_modules__[moduleId].call(...)` where a module uses `this` as its exports (`fixtures/libraries/core-js/webpack5.none.js`) and with the plain call `__webpack_modules__[moduleId](module, module.exports, __webpack_require__)` otherwise (`fixtures/bundle-matrix/base/webpack5-amd/index.js`, which no member of `Function.prototype` sees), and Parcel and Turbopack call their factories through `.call`, so a replaced `Function.prototype.call` sees and can change every module start that goes through it (`e2` in `crates/untwist-cli/tests/browserify_review` makes a module's exports `hooked`), while node starts each written file through its own loader, which does not go through these members. Unpacking assumes, in both lanes, that no code makes such a write and does not look for one. Checking it with the built-ins scan would refuse every browserify tree: on main at c84b42d4 the scan, asked about `Function.prototype.call`, `apply` and `bind`, refused all 46 default-lane trees of the browserify-prelude fixtures and 26 default-lane bundle-matrix cells (12 browserify, 14 webpack), because the runtimes' own computed reads (`n[i]`, `e[i]`, `modules[id]`) count as possible reaches of a prototype. `e1` and `e2` are premise rows in both lanes. The README lists this premise.
- **A browserify module may use only `module.exports` of node's module object.** browser-pack gives each module `{ exports: {} }` and a require function without properties; a written file gets node's `module` (`id`, `filename`, `loaded`, `parent`, `children`, `paths`, `require`) and node's `require` (`cache`, `main`, `resolve`), so `if (!module.parent)` or `require.main === module` take the other branch. A module that reads another property of its `module` or `require` parameter, a computed one, or uses either as a value (anything but `module.exports`, `module["exports"]`, a call of `require` and `typeof`), or that assigns or declares its `require` parameter again (a `var require;` keeps browser-pack's value, so its calls would be linked to the wrong files), means no bundle: `module <id>: it uses module.parent, which browserify does not give its modules and node does; no bundle is written`. The `module` side is the webpack module-object check (`webpack/module_object.rs`) with only `exports` kept; the esbuild and rolldown checks refuse the same uses. The conservative comparison mode keeps the reference deobfuscator's behaviour.
- **A webpack entry that loads chunks is unpacked together with every chunk it loads.** The chunk-loading runtime (the JSONP, `require`, `readFileVm` and `import` loaders, webpack 4's JSONP block, `require.e`, `require.O` and the `require.x` startup with its chunk dependencies, the runtime chunk's deferred start) is accepted only when its text equals a form recorded from real webpack 4/5 output (SHA-256 digests in `webpack/machinery_forms.rs`, the texts in `crates/untwist-unpack/tests/data/webpack_machinery_forms.txt`, regenerated from `fixtures/webpack-variants`, raw and as the unpack stage sees it in each lane, by the ignored test `dump_runtime_forms`), compared after renaming every local by its symbol, reading a `let`/`const` that is never reassigned, never read before its declaration and not inside a loop as `var` (the unpack stage may see either), and abstracting only the installed-chunk table, the chunk-loading global's name, the chunk-id tests of "does this chunk have JS" and the `import()` table of module output. Such a runtime is dropped and `require.e` becomes `function () { return Promise.all([]); }`: every chunk's modules are already in the tree, so a `.then` after it runs a microtask later instead of after a network or file load, and a chunk that would fail to load does not fail. Every chunk a module loads (`require.e(<id>)`) or the startup waits for must be among the inputs or the runtime's installed chunks, or no bundle is written (`module X loads chunk Y, which is not among the inputs`); a computed chunk id refuses the bundle, and so does `require.e` reached any other way than a direct call with one chunk id (an alias, `(0, require.e)(id)`, `.call`/`.apply`, a value) (`reaches its chunk loader other than by calling it with a chunk id`). A module that exists only in chunks loaded lazily (not the entry's chunk, a startup chunk or a chunk the runtime has installed) may be required only where one of its chunks is known to be loaded: inside the first callback of `.then` on `require.e(<id>)` or on `Promise.all([... require.e(<id>) ...])`, or anywhere in a module that only runs after such a load, worked out over the require graph; any other require of it, and any require with a computed id while such modules exist, refuses (`requires module Y where its chunk may not be loaded yet`). This is stricter than node's synchronous `require` chunk loader, under which a chunk is installed as soon as `require.e` is called. A JSONP chunk file merged with a runtime must hold its push and nothing else (directives and empty statements aside), or no bundle is written (`runs code besides its push to the chunk list`). The chunk-loading global (`self.webpackChunk…`) the runtime would create is not created. A module from a chunk is checked against the merged runtime's helpers, so a lone chunk still refuses when it uses a helper (`require.d has no runtime in this input`). webpack 5's development require function with its missing-module check is accepted: a module id outside the bundle then fails with node's error for a missing path rather than webpack's `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` error. A library build (`umd`, `amd`, `system`) gives its entry's exports as the inline entry module's exports (`return __webpack_exports__`); the code around such a bundle must equal a wrapper recorded from webpack 5.24 to 5.112 (`umd`, `umd2`, `amd`, `amd-require`, `system`, named and unnamed, for each `globalObject` webpack writes; the texts in `crates/untwist-unpack/tests/data/webpack_library_heads.txt`, regenerated by `tools/webpack-variants/library-heads.mjs`), compared with the bundle cut out, locals renamed by symbol and the library name abstracted, or no bundle is written (`not a recorded webpack library wrapper`); when the inline entry of such a bundle, or of one that loads chunks, cannot be written as a module, no bundle is written (other bundles keep the entry in the program as before). Not covered yet: webpack 5.24's `deferredModules` startup with `splitChunks`, `output.module` builds whose entry sits at the top level of the module (5.112), module federation, and runtimes minified by uglify or swc (all refused).
- Detection never mutates the input program — module bodies are `CloneIn`-ed — so unpacking no longer has to run after codegen, and a webpack 5 bundle sitting at the top level of a file with no IIFE wrapper is detected, which the reference deobfuscator's `BlockStatement`-keyed visitor cannot see. The webpack 5 container search also backtracks over candidate declarations and requires a non-empty container, so a `var __webpack_module_cache__ = {}` declared before the real container no longer defeats detection.
- An expression-bodied arrow is never accepted as a module factory (the reference deobfuscator builds `t.program(undefined)` from one and crashes), and a var injection whose parameter has no matching argument produces `var x;` instead of crashing the reference deobfuscator's template.
- `-o DIR` with `--force` deletes only an explicit list of files: `deobfuscated.js`, `bundle.json`, the files the current run is about to write, and the module paths recorded in an existing `bundle.json`. No directory is ever removed and nothing recursive happens; the reference deobfuscator's CLI clears the whole output directory recursively.
- Object literals with a single property print on one line (`var x = { Console: bar };`) because `oxc_codegen` only goes multi-line above one property, where Babel always breaks. This is a printer difference and disappears under `xtask::diff::normalize`.
- A user path-mapping key is a literal path exactly when it starts with `.` (not only `./`): `resolve_mapping_path` in `mappings.rs` refuses `../escape.js` as unsafe instead of turning it into `node_modules/../escape.js`, because `PosixPath::parse` rejects any normalised path starting with `../` regardless of how the key was written.
- A module whose derived or resolved path is refused by `PosixPath::parse` gets the `_unsafe_<id>.js` fallback from `fallback_path` plus a `Note` (`module <id>: unsafe path <source> replaced by <path>`) from `assign_paths`, and this holds after a chunk merge retags a module's entry id too: `Module::assign_default_path` is the single place that derives a path, applies the fallback and records `unsafe_path_source`, so `Module::new` and `merge_bundles`'s retagging both go through it and both re-emit the note.
- `-o DIR` refuses to write or `--force`-delete through any symlink component below DIR (DIR itself may be a symlink): `writer::symlink_free` walks every path segment below DIR with `symlink_metadata` and refuses if any is a symlink, and `writer::is_contained` canonicalizes the deepest existing ancestor of the target and requires it to stay under DIR; both `write_all` and `clean` (the `--force` deletion path) are gated by this and report each refusal instead of writing or deleting through it, excluding it from `files_written`. The reference deobfuscator's CLI only throws on lexical `..` traversal at save time and has no symlink awareness at all.
- The `symlink_free`/`is_contained` containment check is check-then-act, not atomic: an attacker able to write inside DIR while `untwist -o DIR` is running can still race it. `write_all` writes each file through a same-directory temp file and `rename`, so a hard link planted at the target path no longer leaks the write into the link's other name (`rename` replaces DIR's own directory entry and leaves the other name alone), and a symlink planted at the target's own leaf position isn't followed by `rename` either. The residual gap is an intermediate path segment (a directory component, not the leaf) that is swapped for a symlink between the check and the write: `NamedTempFile::new_in` and the following `rename` both re-resolve that segment at call time and would follow it. Closing this fully needs `O_NOFOLLOW`/`openat`-based path resolution, which is out of scope here.
- **The webpack entry marker is `.s`, and nothing else.** The reference deobfuscator matches only
  `__webpack_require__.s` (`unpack/webpack/common-matchers.ts:143`); its own closed-unmerged PR #34
  proposed adding `.j`, but `.j` is webpack 5's `RuntimeGlobals.chunkId` — the id of the chunk currently
  executing, never an entry module id — which is exactly why that PR was closed rather than merged:
  `fixtures/reference/unpack/webpack-5-no-entry.js` assigns `__webpack_require__.j = 377` for
  `installedChunks['377']`, and `377` names no module. Untwist rules `.j` out alongside the issue's other
  four names — `.e`, `.d`, `.m` and `.r`, the ensure-chunk, define, module-table and `__esModule`-setter
  helpers — and pins the collision case (a chunk id that happens to equal a real module id) in
  `fixtures/unpack-gaps/webpack-5-chunk-id-j.js`, so a chunk id is never read as the entry even when it
  matches one.
- **A startup body with several top-level `require(id)` calls is refused.** The reference deobfuscator
  takes the first as the entry silently (`common-matchers.ts:157-164`), which is what reference deobfuscator
  issue #68 objects to, and the written files then run only that module. By default Untwist refuses a prelude
  that starts more than one entry module (several top-level `require(id)` calls, or one beside a webpack 5
  inline entry IIFE): `the prelude is not proven to be webpack's runtime; no bundle is written: the prelude
  starts more than one entry module`. A single top-level `require(id)` is the entry in webpack 4 and 5. The
  conservative comparison mode keeps the first id and the note naming the count
  (`Bundle::entry_candidates`), so the uncertainty is visible there.
- **A Promise-based chunk-loading runtime's entry id now comes from its `.O` registration.**
  webpack 5's `output.chunkLoading: "require"` runtime (`__webpack_require__.O`/`.f.require`
  against an `installedChunks` map, reference deobfuscator issue #33) still pushes its modules through the same
  `self["webpackChunk…"]` global the JSONP detector already matches, so measuring against
  `fixtures/unpack-gaps/webpack-5-promise-chunk.js` found the modules and chunk ids correctly and
  only `entry_id` came back `None` — nothing read the `.O(0, [chunk], () => require(id))` call that
  names the chunk's requested module. `registered_entry_id`/`required_id` in `chunk.rs` read it from
  the first such registration anywhere in the program's top-level statements (unwrapping a top-level
  `SequenceExpression`'s elements, since minifiers chain several `.O(...)` calls with the comma
  operator, and following both arrow-body forms — expression and block — since minifiers emit
  either).
- **the reference deobfuscator's closed-unmerged PR #50 shapes are fixtures now.** Its two webpack 4
  shapes are built by webpack 4.47.0 from the shared app: `fixtures/unpack-bundlers/webpack/webpack4-dev-paths.js`
  (readable `./app/…` ids, `__webpack_require__.t` around a JSON import) and `webpack4-externals.js`
  (a factory calling the host's own `require("path")`). Both unpack, and the written modules run
  under node with the bundle's output. The host `require` stays the host's (see below);
  `require.t(id, 9)` becomes `require(id)`; every other `.t` mode, and webpack's `.r/.d/.o/.n` where a
  module keeps them, are taken verbatim from the bundle's own prelude into `_runtime/webpack.js`
  behind a synthesized `__webpack_require__(id) = require(<path>)`.
- **the reference deobfuscator's ESM conversion runs only where it is proven.** The reference deobfuscator
  turns every harmony module into ESM: a numeric harmony import of a CommonJS target becomes
  `import * as x` (the namespace lacks the target's properties), a `.d` on a namespace object
  becomes `export const` (the namespace stays empty), a getter becomes an eager `export let`, and
  imports hoist above earlier effects. By default Untwist writes `export`s only for a module whose
  conversion is proven (strict, harmony, `.d` only on `exports` with getters reading distinct
  top-level bindings, no leftover `exports`/`module`/`this`/`arguments`, no require cycle, no
  `__esModule` observation, no interop target, every consumer a plain member read) and keeps its
  `require`s, so evaluation order is unchanged; every other module stays CommonJS with its helpers
  in `_runtime/webpack.js`. The webpack 5 inline entry is written as `index.js` under the same
  rules. In a bootstrap that is strict code, an inline entry IIFE without its own `"use strict"`
  counts as the entry only right after the entry's exports object (`let __webpack_exports__ = {};`),
  as webpack writes it when every module is strict; it is written with `"use strict"`. The conservative comparison mode keeps the reference deobfuscator's conversion, so `diff-unpack` is unchanged; several default
  the reference deobfuscator snapshots were re-pinned for it.

- **A factory parameter is not renamed onto a name its body already reads free.**
  the reference deobfuscator renames webpack's `(e, t, i)` and browserify's factory parameters to `module`,
  `exports` and `require` even when the body also reads the host's own `require` (or `module`,
  `exports`): `require.hmd(e)` beside `i.d(t, …)` becomes `require.hmd(e)` beside `require.d(…)`,
  so the host's reference is captured by the runtime's and node sees a different program
  (`crates/untwist/tests/host_require.rs` runs both). Untwist gives such a parameter a fresh name
  (`_require`) instead; the conservative comparison mode keeps the reference deobfuscator's fold, so `diff-unpack` is unchanged. The default
  snapshot of `fixtures/reference/unpack/webpack-esm.js` was re-pinned for it.

### Bundlers the reference deobfuscator does not unpack

The reference deobfuscator detects only webpack and browserify (its issue #117). Untwist also splits the bundlers
below. Every kind follows one contract: a written module set must behave like the bundle under
node, or no bundle is written and the whole program is output as before, with the note
`unpack: <kind> bundle shape found but not proven; no bundle is written`. A refusal is never a
failure; the shapes each kind accepts and refuses are pinned by `fixtures/unpack-bundlers/`
(generated by the real bundlers at exact versions, plus hand-written `min-`/`neg-` shapes) and run
under node by `cargo xtask diff-unpack-behaviour` in default and unpack-only modes.
`bundle.json`'s `"type"` names the kind in lower case (`esbuild`, `rollup`, `systemjs`, `amd`,
`umd`, `parcel`, `metro`, `turbopack`, `closure`).

- **Detection order.** The reference deobfuscator's four detectors run first, unchanged, then Closure's module
  manager, SystemJS, esbuild (Bun's wrapper unwrapped first), Metro, Parcel and Turbopack, then a
  UMD/AMD/SystemJS wrapper's single module is run back through the splitting kinds (an esbuild
  bundle inside UMD splits), then AMD/UMD itself. Rollup/Vite scope hoisting runs last and only
  when asked (below). The new probes look only at the top-level statements and one wrapper body,
  so a non-bundle input is not re-parsed.
- **Output form.** A CommonJS factory becomes a module with its own body and CJS names; an
  ESM-shaped module (SystemJS, a Rollup split) is written as ESM; esbuild's lazy `__esm` init stays
  a lazy exported `init_x` function, because lazy-once is not import hoisting. A path-like id the
  bundler recorded (esbuild keys or `// path` comments, SystemJS names, AMD ids, Parcel and
  Turbopack asset paths) becomes the module's path through the usual traversal and collision
  checks; otherwise `<id>.js`. The entry is `index.js`, reserved even against a module whose own id
  is `index` (that module gets `index-2.js`).
- **The runtime module.** A helper whose semantics are not `require`'s (esbuild's
  `__toESM`/`__esm`, webpack's `.t`, Parcel's hoisted helpers) is moved verbatim from the bundle
  into `_runtime/<kind>.js`, which the modules that use it require; it must itself be closed (only
  globals and other helpers free), hold no `with`, and read none of the host names below, which
  every written file has for itself. A moved esbuild binding that is assigned after its declaration
  (the `var` an `__esm` init fills) is exported through a getter, and the modules read it as
  `runtime.name` each time, a call as `(0, runtime.name)()`; a bundle that deletes such a name,
  assigns it outside the runtime module or names it where only a binding fits (an `export { name }`,
  a `for (name in …)` target) is not unpacked, and two inputs whose runtime exports such a getter
  are not linked into one bundle. esbuild's lazy helpers, the names getter they call and the
  `__require` shim are trusted only while each is declared once and never assigned. Metro's `importDefault`/`importAll` live inside Metro's polyfill
  closure, so `_runtime/metro.js` holds a synthesized `metroRequire(id)` plus copies of Metro's two
  interop functions. Closure's shared `var`s live in a null-prototype holder,
  `_runtime/closure.js`.
- **Free host names are never renamed, and never captured.** A factory that reads a free
  `require`, `module`, `exports`, `__filename` or `__dirname` the bundler did not map is refused
  (except a bare `require("pkg")` of a host package, which is kept as the host's), since the
  written file would see a different value.
- **Wrapper names a module declares itself are renamed.** A factory body (or an unwrapped entry)
  that declares `require`, `module`, `exports`, `__filename` or `__dirname` itself, where that name
  is not one of the factory's own parameters, gets the binding renamed (`_require`, ...) in the
  written CommonJS file: node's wrapper binds those names, so a `let` would no longer parse and an
  uninitialised `var` would read the wrapper's value instead of `undefined`.
- **A factory parameter renamed to `require`, `module` or `exports` moves every binding of that
  name aside.** When a factory parameter takes the name (webpack, browserify, Parcel, Turbopack,
  esbuild, Metro, the webpack require shield and the shared-runtime fold), every binding of that
  name anywhere in the module gets a fresh name (`_require`, `_require2`, ...), not only the one
  nearest a use, so an outer `function f(require)` around an inner one cannot capture the new
  `require` call. Where the binding cannot be proven, the bundle is refused with `a factory
  parameter would be renamed to a name bound inside the module where the binding cannot be proven
  (...); not unpacked`: a catch parameter beside a sloppy block function of the same name (the
  parser binds the block's reads to the catch parameter), a `var` redeclaring a catch parameter
  that the parser binds to the wrong scope, a direct `eval` or `with` statement inside the scope
  of such a binding, or a use of the parameter inside a direct `eval` or `with` scope. A direct
  `eval` here, and in every other unpack check, is any call spelled `eval(...)`, however `eval` is
  bound: sloppy code may bind the name (`var eval = globalThis.eval`, `let eval`, a parameter or
  `catch (eval)`), and such a call is still a direct eval when the binding holds the global `eval`.
  Rows: `crates/untwist/tests/unpack_factory_name_rows.rs`, both lanes, node parity.
- **esbuild's `__require` shim in an ES-module bundle.** Without the `createRequire` banner the
  shim finds no `require` and throws "Dynamic require ... is not supported"; such a bundle is not
  split, since a written CommonJS file would load the module instead.
- **Rollup/Vite scope hoisting is opt-in: `--split-hoisted`.** A hoisted bundle has no module
  boundaries of its own, so the split is a heuristic over the wrapper's top-level declarations
  (clusters by reference adjacency, a binding's writers kept with its owner). It is refused for a
  sloppy wrapper, any top-level statement besides the wrapper, any `currentScript` read, and any
  binding written across a module edge. `game.js` reads `document.currentScript` and is therefore
  not split. A function declared more than once at the wrapper's top level keeps its last
  declaration only, the one every reference in the wrapper sees; a name declared twice in any other
  way (a `var` beside a function) is refused, since an ES module may not declare a name twice.
- **`--split-assume-modules` (with `--split-hoisted`) assumes the split tree is ES modules for
  reading and for running in node.** It does not preserve `document.currentScript` (an ES module
  sees `null`), classic-script synchronous load timing, or sloppy-mode top-level semantics. With
  it, Rollup's iife `import.meta.url` stand-in
  (`var x = typeof document != "undefined" ? document.currentScript : null`) no longer refuses the
  split and stays in the entry as written, and the bundle may sit one function below the program
  top level, inside an outer wrapper whose other statements are `var` declarations (and, when the
  outer function is strict, function declarations and code after the bundle). The plan is not the
  heuristic: every @rollup/plugin-commonjs `requireX` wrapper, with its flag and its exports
  holder, becomes its own module; Rollup's own helpers that those wrappers read
  (`commonjsGlobal` and other side-effect-free declarations) go to `chunk_shared.js`; everything
  else stays in the entry, in order. A wrapper module only holds declarations that run no code
  (function declarations, `var`s with no value or a plain literal, object or array value), so
  importing it before the entry runs changes nothing; a value is only moved when nothing can read
  it before its original line. A wrapper that reads code left in the entry, is written from
  outside, or would be shadowed by an outer-wrapper name stays in the entry, and so does a wrapper
  whose names the outer wrapper's own code reads (the entry's new imports would otherwise capture
  those reads). Outer code that reads `module`, `require`, `exports`, `__filename`, `__dirname`
  or `import.meta` refuses the split, and so does `this` in the code of an arrow outer wrapper.
  `undefined`, `NaN` and `Infinity` count as plain values only where no binding shadows them.
  Outer-wrapper
  bindings a wrapper module reads come from a generated `shell.js` that exports them as live
  bindings: they must be declared without a value, the bundle may not write them, and the outer
  code may assign them only after the bundle with `x = e;` or `var x = e;` statements, which the
  entry routes through a setter exported by `shell.js` (`set_x(x = e)`). Under the flag the
  lexical stage keeps `var`s that later closures read (the split reads Rollup's `var` holders), and
  once the bundle is split, `var`-to-`let`/`const` runs again on each written module, where each
  module is its own scope; `deobfuscated.js`, written beside the tree, keeps those `var`s. Without
  the flag nothing changes.
- **Inferred ES-module boundaries under `--split-assume-modules`.** What stays in the entry is cut
  into contiguous runs of statements, one file per run, at points where Rollup's module order
  shows through: a frozen namespace object (`Object.freeze({ __proto__: null, ... })`) ends a run
  and holds the declarations it lists; a run boundary needs the earlier run to be read from later
  code while the two runs neither share most of their readers nor most of the earlier bindings
  they read, or a later run declaring a name the earlier one also declares up to Rollup's `$N`
  suffix. The boundaries are a guess and only change the layout: the runs keep the bundle's
  statement order (the entry imports the last run first and every run imports the one before it
  first, so the module graph evaluates them in bundle order), a statement that reads a later
  binding stays in one run with it, and everything from the first statement that needs the
  wrapper function (`this`, `arguments`, `return`, an outer-wrapper name, a name the outer wrapper
  also declares) to the end stays in the entry. A binding assigned from another run with a plain
  `x = e` is exported with a setter (`set_x(e)`, or `set_x({ x: e }.x)` when `e` is an anonymous
  function or class, which keeps its inferred name); any other write from another run (`+=`,
  `++`, destructuring, `for (x in ...)`) keeps the writer and the declaration in one run. A run is
  named after the first class or function another module imports from it, else `module<N>`. An
  outer wrapper may now also declare `let`/`const` names; those are never exported through
  `shell.js`, so a wrapper module that reads them stays in the entry. Expected quality, scored against
  Rollup's own source map on fixtures/unpack-rollup-boundaries (rollup 3/4, see `SCORES`):
  boundary precision 0.78 and recall 0.48 overall; three.js 0.79/0.68 plain and 0.96/0.66
  minified, Svelte 5 0.67/0.38 plain and 1.00/0.31 minified, Solid 0.50/0.25 plain (solid-js is
  one large module), the synthetic app 0.67/0.50 plain; the terser-minified Solid and synthetic
  apps stay one file (terser moves code between modules). Boundaries lean to under-splitting. The
  inference is the `boundaries` cargo feature, on by default in the CLI and in the wasm build
  (the playground's Assume ES modules setting).
- **Closure.** Only the module manager's `try {…} catch (e) { X._DumpException(e) }` segments
  are split (ids from `/*_M:id*/` markers or begin/end loader calls checked against the
  `_ModuleManager_initialize` graph). The namespace object is read once, in
  `_runtime/closure.js`, and every file gets that one object as its wrapper parameter, as the
  bundle binds it once; a segment that assigns or deletes the namespace property on the global
  object (`window._ = …`, `this._ = …`) is refused. A `var x = this` line of the wrapper is copied
  only into the files that name `x`. Closure ADVANCED property renaming stays a non-goal. A Closure
  bundle inside a UMD or AMD factory is not re-fed: its top-level `this` is the factory's receiver,
  which an AMD loader sets to `exports`. Every written segment runs with `globalThis` as its
  top-level `this`, which is what the bundle's `this` is in a browser classic script. This is an
  accepted assumption: required as a CommonJS file under node the bundle's `this` is
  `module.exports`, so there a bundle that reaches globals through `var window = this` and its
  output differ.
- **esbuild.** A bundle is split only when every `__commonJS` factory is declared before any
  statement at its level can run code: up to the last factory declaration only helpers, function
  declarations, imports and `var`s whose values are functions or plain literals may stand, so no
  `require_x()` can run while `require_x` is still `undefined`. The lazy helper may not bind a name
  that its body reads (`function mod()`, a `catch (mod)`, a parameter named `eval` or `arguments`,
  the names getter as a parameter); the keyed form needs a free `Object`, and a factory keyed
  `__proto__` is refused. A factory in method form that uses `super` at its own level is refused,
  since the written module is no longer a method.
- **Metro.** Factories with 5 or 6 parameters (Metro < 0.52) are refused. `__d` and `__r` are
  Metro's only when the file shows it: the prelude must hold Metro's `require.js` polyfill, equal
  after α-renaming to a recorded text (`metro/runtimes/`, metro 0.87.2 production, not
  minified, as written and as the default and `--unsafe` passes leave it), `__METRO_GLOBAL_PREFIX__` must be bound once to the prefix the calls use, no other
  prelude statement may spell a name ending in `__d` or `__r`, and the statements after the prelude
  may call nothing at their own level but those two. A prelude that defines the names any other way
  is refused, a minified or older runtime included, until its text is recorded. A file with no
  prelude (the names are free, as in a split or lazy bundle) is refused in the safe lane and
  unpacked with `--unsafe`, which takes the names on trust. A prelude polyfill that replaces the
  loader without spelling its name (through a computed key) is not seen. Module ids keep their type,
  as in Metro's `Map`: every definition, dependency entry and `__r` target must be all numbers or all
  strings, and an id `__proto__` or `index` is refused. A literal `require` argument of the other type
  is left to `metroRequire`, whose table is a `Map` and which throws Metro's "Requiring unknown module"
  for an id it does not hold.
- **SystemJS.** The entry is the first named register (SystemJS's named-register extension never
  instantiates an anonymous register beside named ones). Setters must be plain binding, namespace or
  re-export forms, and static cycles are refused; `_context.meta` is refused rather than mapped to
  `import.meta`, whose `url` depends on the file's location. An `execute() {}` method that uses
  `super` at its own level is refused.
- **Bun.** Bun's CommonJS wrapper `(function (exports, require, module, __filename, __dirname) {…})`
  is unwrapped only when the file starts with Bun's `// @bun @bun-cjs` pragma (after a hashbang
  line at most), which is what makes Bun call the function; the file is read as Bun runs it.
  Without the pragma the expression is left as written, and an `async` wrapper is not Bun's.
- **AMD and UMD.** AMD needs every top-level statement to be a `define`, all anonymous (one) or all named;
  dependency cycles, loader plugins (`!`), the `define(function (require) {…})` sugar and a `module`
  dependency are refused. A UMD wrapper's non-factory arguments must be inert (`this`, a literal,
  a `typeof X !== "undefined" ? X : …` guard). The wrapper's branch is chosen from `typeof define`
  tests only: a bare `define` read (`if (define && define.amd)`) throws where `define` is not
  declared, so such a wrapper is refused. The wrapper must be a plain function or arrow
  (not `async`) with distinct parameter names, and a factory or `define` callback that repeats a
  parameter name is refused.
- **Parcel.** Both runtimes are accepted, the registry (`--no-scope-hoist`) only when its runtime
  text matches one of five recorded forms after α-renaming (`parcel/runtimes/`; if a later
  prepare or unminify change rewrites that runtime differently, Parcel registry bundles are refused
  until the forms are re-recorded). Dependency maps with a repeated or `__proto__` key are refused.
  A require that is neither a module of the bundle nor a node builtin is refused: Parcel externals
  are not accepted, which also keeps an `Object.prototype` name (`require("constructor")`, which
  Parcel's runtime resolves through the prototype) from being read as an external. Accepting
  externals later must exclude those names explicitly. The registry call must pass no more
  arguments than its runtime takes; without the fifth (externals) argument the runtime throws on
  any name outside the bundle, so a builtin require is refused there. A builtin require and
  `module.bundle.root(...)` both go through the global `parcelRequire<hash>` slot at run time, so
  a bundle that uses either is refused when a factory can replace that slot: a write to a property
  of that name, the global object (`globalThis`, `global`, `self`, `window`, the factory's fourth
  parameter, `Function`, indirect `eval`) used other than as `G.name`, `G["name"]`, `typeof G` or
  in an equality test, or a write through a computed key on it or on a nested function's `this`.
  An alias of a nested function's `this` is not followed. A lazy chunk that the inputs
  supply is linked into one bundle. A hoisted `var` helper is moved to `_runtime/parcel.js` only
  when no earlier top-level statement names it; otherwise it stays where it is. The scope-hoisted form is accepted only when the statement that
  defines `parcelRequire` equals a recorded text after α-renaming (Parcel 2.16.4, development
  and minified, each as written and as prepare and unminify leave it), and `$parcel$modules` and `$parcel$inits` are each declared once as
  `{}` and named nowhere else at the top level; another Parcel version's definition is refused
  until its text is recorded.
- **Turbopack.** Browser chunks with a registration naming their runtime entries, and server chunks
  given together with Next's page loader and `[turbopack]_runtime.js`, are split. A browser chunk
  holds no runtime, so it is read as if Turbopack's standard runtime loads it, and every such
  unpack prints a note saying so; a chunk the standard runtime would not run that way is refused,
  such as a registration pushed before a module list. A chunk whose
  factories use Turbopack's interop, async or chunk-loading helpers (`i`, `s`, `A`, `l`, …) is
  refused: those helpers live only in the runtime file, so they cannot be moved. Browser multi-chunk
  input is refused (no node oracle).
- **A throwing factory is re-run.** Parcel's and Turbopack's runtimes (like webpack 4's, Metro's and browser-pack's,
  as before) keep a module that threw cached; node's `require` deletes the cache entry and re-runs it. esbuild's
  `__commonJS` resets like node and is exact.
- **Several input files are one program.** Unpack never sees the input file
  names, only their texts, so a chunk load (Parcel's `module.require("./lazy.<hash>.js")`, Next's
  loader `R.c(...)`) is linked to the input that defines the ids it names, not to the file the
  specifier names. This is the premise webpack's JSONP chunk merge already used. If the inputs are
  not the whole program, a load that would have read some other file is resolved to the given
  input with the same ids; a load whose ids no input defines refuses the group. Passing input
  names through to unpack, so the specifiers can be checked, is not in 5e. The premise covers only
  chunks a loader loads: Next's page loader must load exactly as many chunks as are given (each
  named once), and a module of a Parcel chunk may be required only by the loader that loads its
  chunk (inside the loader's `.then`); a require of it from anywhere else, which in the bundle
  could run before the chunk exists, refuses the group. A chunk's own modules may require the
  root bundle's modules, which exist before any chunk loads.

### WebAssembly glue

- **An extracted wasm module stays in the code.** With `--wasm-check auto` or `on` and `-o`, a
  byte array, base64 text or `data:` URI that holds a whole module is written to `wasm/`, and the
  literal is left where it is: the program may read it as data (its length, a slice, a hash) or
  hand it to `WebAssembly.Module`, which takes bytes, not a path. The literal is replaced by the
  relative path of the written file (`"./wasm/<name>.wasm"`) only where its one use is a loader
  that also takes a URL: a `data:application/wasm` or `data:application/octet-stream` URI that is
  the first argument of a call of the global `fetch`. That output then fetches the file, so it
  runs where the written file is served beside it at that path; `fetch` resolves a relative URL
  against the page, not the script.
- **Glue names keep the bindings other code can reach.** In a classic script (no `import` or
  `export`) a top-level `var` or function is a property of the global object that later scripts
  read by name, so the wasm glue renamer leaves those names alone, as the main renamer does when
  it keeps script globals. A block-level function declaration in sloppy code and the `var` of the
  same name that it writes (Annex B) also keep their names, and so does such a function when
  code outside its block reads the name. Glue inside a function, in an ES module or in an
  unpacked module file is named as before.

- **Unpacking keeps the name a bundle gives a function.** Always in the default lane, with or without `--rename` (no scan can tell that a program never reads `name`, see rename.md); under `--unsafe` only when the bundle or another input reads `name` as the scan sees it: Closure Library's shared `var x = function () {}`, written as a member of `__closure_vars`, becomes `__closure_vars.x = { x: function () {} }.x`, so it is still named `x`; SystemJS `_export("double", function () {})`, written as `double = …`, becomes `double = (0, function () {})`, so it stays unnamed. A webpack var-injection argument that is an anonymous function, class or arrow is always written as `var a = (0, function () {})`, since a parameter gives its argument no name. The same holds for the other forms: a Closure shared variable assigned later (`x = function () {}`, `x ||= …`, `x ??= …`, `x &&= …`) becomes `__closure_vars.x = { x: function () {} }.x`; a SystemJS declarator export (`var x = _export("x", function () {})`, Rollup's `system` output) becomes `var x = (0, function () {})`; a SystemJS object-form export (`_export({ default: function () {} })`) whose name cannot be a binding refuses the bundle, since its local would be named `$default`. When a factory's parameters are renamed to `module`, `exports` and `require` (webpack, esbuild, browserify, Parcel, Turbopack, Metro) and that moves a name off an anonymous function, class or arrow (an inner `var exports = function () {}` that becomes `_exports`, or `e = function () {}` with `e` the exports parameter), the value is written as `{ exports: function () {} }.exports` (`{ e: … }.e`) so it keeps the name the bundle gives it; a class declaration is written `let _exports = class exports {}` when nothing inside the class names it; a function declaration, such a class whose body names it, or a named function or class expression whose name would change refuses the bundle (`a module binding that gives a function its name would be renamed while the bundle may read names; not unpacked`), including when the rename happens after detection (webpack's require shield, two runtimes folded into one). A rename made for a collision never takes a name the module reads as a free name, so it cannot capture the runtime's `require`; a use of the runtime `require` the conversion leaves (`typeof n`) is written as `require`, node's, like in a module without the shield. A module, or a webpack entry inlined after the runtime, that reads `bind`, `call` or `apply` off its runtime require (`n.bind(n, 3)`, webpack's own lazy-import form) means no bundle in the default lane (an inlined entry is left in `deobfuscated.js`) (`require.bind would hand out node's require, whose name differs`): the bound function's `name` is `bound o` in the bundle and `bound require` in the written file. Under `--unsafe` `n.bind(n, id)` is written as `require.bind(require, "./id.js")`. The webpack comparison mode (`convert_esm`, test builds only) applies the same wrappers.
